chapter_title: Analog Output: PWM and Controlling Brightness, Speed, and Tone

screens.title: Analog Output with PWM
screens.subtitle: How Arduino simulates analog signals to control brightness, speed, and tone

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn how the Arduino Uno creates usable analog-like outputs without a digital-to-analog converter. The board uses pulse width modulation, or PWM, which rapidly switches a pin on and off so the average voltage seen by an LED, motor, or servo changes. You will see how the duty cycle maps to perceived brightness and speed, learn which pins support PWM on the Uno, and practise using the analogWrite and tone commands to build fading LEDs and simple sounds. We'll also contrast PWM with a true DAC and explain when you need a real analog output. A short hands-on activity uses a potentiometer to control LED brightness and triggers a buzzer when brightness passes a threshold. By the end you'll understand how a stream of on/off pulses can become smooth control in everyday circuits, why transistors or drivers are required for motors, and how audible PWM can be for some loads. Think about a fan you can slow down smoothly — PWM is what makes that control practical on most Arduinos.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: PWM creates an average voltage from rapid on/off pulses; duty cycle controls the effective voltage and therefore brightness, speed, or tonal output.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this lesson

narration.text: These four objectives map how you will learn to use PWM on the Arduino Uno. First, you will understand pulse width modulation: what a duty cycle is, how frequency affects perception, and why averaging pulses produces a usable voltage. Second, you will be able to call the analogWrite function to set a value between zero and two hundred fifty-five to change brightness and motor speed, and identify the Uno pins that support PWM. Third, you will perform practical tasks: fading an LED smoothly, controlling a motor through a transistor or driver, and positioning simple servos where applicable. Fourth, you will use tone and noTone to generate short beeps and melodies on a piezo buzzer and understand their limits for audio. Each objective pairs skill with a short practice so you prove competency, and each builds toward safely controlling actuators in projects. Keep in mind a common misconception: analogWrite does not produce a steady analog voltage; it produces a timed pulse train whose average is the useful part. That distinction will guide when you choose a DAC or an alternative board.

screens.title: Objectives — Practice & Safety
screens.subtitle: Practical skills and common safety checks for outputs

narration.text: This second objectives slide focuses on hands-on practice and safe wiring. You should be able to wire an LED with a current-limiting resistor and fade it smoothly, and wire a DC motor through a transistor or motor driver so the Arduino never directly sources motor current. You will practice reading a potentiometer and mapping its value to analogWrite so brightness responds in real time. For sound, you'll connect a piezo buzzer and play short beep sequences, then stop them using noTone. Each practice includes safety checks: confirm shared ground between components, use proper resistors for LEDs, and add a flyback diode when switching motors. A frequent misconception is thinking PWM raises or lowers the pin voltage permanently; instead it changes the average delivered energy over time. These practical habits prevent burnt components and unreliable behavior, and they prepare you to scale from LEDs to actuators without damaging your board.

screens.title: What is PWM and Duty Cycle?
screens.subtitle: Define pulse width modulation and how duty cycle sets average voltage

narration.text: Pulse width modulation is the method the Arduino Uno uses to simulate different voltage levels by switching a digital pin rapidly between on and off. The key quantity is the duty cycle, which is the fraction or percent of the cycle time the signal is on. For example, when the signal is on for half the cycle and off for the other half, the duty cycle is fifty percent and the effective average voltage at a five volt Arduino will be approximately two point five volts. Frequency is the speed of these cycles; typical Arduino PWM frequency on most Uno pins is about four hundred ninety hertz, which is fast enough that an LED appears to hold constant brightness, while slower devices might perceive flicker. A common misconception is to think analogWrite sets a voltage; instead, analogWrite sets a duty-cycle value between zero and two hundred fifty-five. A concrete example: calling analogWrite on pin nine with a value near one hundred twenty-eight produces about fifty percent duty cycle, which produces a mid-level brightness on an LED. Remember that the device connected responds to the average energy delivered over time. Takeaway: PWM is time-domain averaging, not a true variable voltage. How would your project change if you needed precise steady voltages instead of averaged pulses?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: PWM toggles a pin on and off; duty cycle is the percent of time on and determines the effective average voltage.

Pulse Width Modulation
Time-domain technique that creates an average voltage by turning a pin on and off rapidly.
Core idea

Example

Common mistake
Thinking analogWrite outputs a steady voltage. It sets pulse timing instead; the device senses the average.
Key Takeaway

PWM uses time to change effective voltage. Duty cycle is the control knob you use.

Terms: Duty cycle, frequency, average voltage.

screens.title: Using analogWrite to Fade an LED
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step approach to smooth fades with mapped potentiometer input

narration.text: Fading an LED is one of the clearest uses of PWM. The process begins by reading a control input, like a potentiometer on an analog input. The raw analog reading ranges across the ADC values; map that reading into the PWM range zero to two hundred fifty-five so it becomes a valid value for analogWrite. Apply analogWrite to a PWM-capable pin that is connected to your LED through a current-limiting resistor. To produce a visible smooth fade, increment or decrement the PWM value in small steps with short delays between steps; a delay of around ten milliseconds produces smooth motion without blocking too long. A concrete example is increasing brightness from zero to full by sending a sequence of values from zero up to two hundred fifty-five, then back down. A common misconception is to put the LED on directly without a resistor — that risks excessive current and possible damage. Also, avoid connecting the LED to a non-PWM pin and expecting a fade; it will be either on or off. Takeaway: map inputs to the right numeric range, use safe wiring, and choose step timing to balance smoothness and responsiveness. How would you modify the loop to respond instantly to a changing potentiometer instead of a timed sweep?

screens.title: PWM vs True DAC
screens.subtitle: When PWM is sufficient and when you need a proper DAC

narration.text: PWM and digital-to-analog converters both produce effects that look like analog voltages, but they do so in different ways and suit different needs. PWM approximates analog output by changing the average energy delivered over time; it is ideal for LEDs, many motors, and hobby servos because these devices respond to average voltage or pulse width rather than a precise steady voltage. A true DAC, in contrast, outputs a steady voltage level continuously; you need a DAC for high-fidelity audio or precision control systems where the instantaneous voltage must not fluctuate. An example: an LED dimmer or motor speed control usually works perfectly with PWM, while an audio output chain for music playback needs a DAC for low distortion. A common misunderstanding is assuming PWM frequency is unimportant; frequency matters because low frequency can cause visible flicker or audible motor noise. If your project requires stable voltages or very low ripple, choose an external DAC module or a board like a microcontroller with built-in analog outputs. Takeaway: match the method to the component's sensitivity to ripple and the precision your application requires.

keyIdea.title: Contrast
keyIdea.text: PWM averages pulses over time; DACs produce steady voltages. Use PWM for actuators, DACs for precision analog or high-quality audio.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › PWM vs True DAC
When PWM is enough
LED dimming, motor speed control, and hobby servos usually work well with PWM because they react to average power.
  • Simple brightness control for LEDs
  • DC motor speed control when using a transistor or driver
  • Positioning hobby servos that accept pulse widths
When you need a DAC
Audio playback, precision analog sensors, or low-ripple control loops require steady voltages a DAC provides.
Example
A music player needs a DAC to avoid the switching noise and harmonic content that PWM introduces.
Common misconception
Believing higher PWM values increase actual pin voltage. They change the on-time only; the instantaneous voltage is still rail when on and zero when off.
Key Takeaway

Choose PWM for actuators; choose a DAC when stable, low-noise analog voltages are required.

screens.title: PWM Pins on the Arduino Uno
screens.subtitle: Which pins support PWM and how they are marked

narration.text: On the Arduino Uno only certain digital pins provide hardware PWM. These are pins three, five, six, nine, ten, and eleven. On the physical board each of these pins is marked with a tilde symbol to indicate PWM capability. Knowing which pins can generate PWM is important because analogWrite on a non-PWM pin will not produce a true pulse-width-modulated signal; it will only write a digital value that is either on or off. Practical example: choose pin nine when following many common tutorials that fade an LED, because examples and shields often assume that pin. A common mistake is to assume every digital pin behaves identically for analogWrite. While some boards emulate PWM in software on other pins, the Uno only supports hardware PWM on the listed pins and that hardware provides stable frequency and timing. Takeaway: use the marked PWM pins for reliable analogWrite behavior and consult the board markings if you are unsure. PWM Pins on the Arduino Uno means pwm-capable pins on the uno: 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11 — marked with a tilde on the board.. In practical terms, which pins support pwm and how they are marked. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: analogWrite Values and Mapping
screens.subtitle: How analogWrite values 0–255 map to perceived output and how to compute average voltage

narration.text: The analogWrite function on the Arduino accepts a value from zero up to two hundred fifty-five. Zero corresponds to always off and two hundred fifty-five to always on. Values between produce a duty cycle equal to value divided by two hundred fifty-five. For practical thinking, multiply that fraction by five volts on a standard Uno to estimate the average voltage the load sees. For example, a value of sixty-four corresponds to about sixty-four over two hundred fifty-five times five volts, which is roughly one point two five volts average. Use this mapping to make decisions when you need a specific effective voltage for a sensor or to estimate motor torque at a given setting. In practice you rarely need exact voltages for LEDs. When you do need accurate analog levels, consider smoothing the PWM with a low-pass filter or using a DAC. A common error is sending values that expect different voltage rails; remember the five volt reference on the Uno influences the average. Takeaway: think of analogWrite as a percentage knob and do the arithmetic to estimate average voltage when precision matters.

keyIdea.title: Mapping
keyIdea.text: analogWrite values map to duty cycle as value/255; multiply that by Vcc to estimate the average voltage.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › analogWrite Values and Mapping
Value mapping
Use the proportion value divided by two hundred fifty-five to compute duty cycle and average voltage.
// Conceptual math // dutyCycle = value / 255 // averageVoltage ≈ dutyCycle × 5V // Example: value 64 → average ≈ 64/255 × 5V ≈ 1.25V
Concrete example
Set analogWrite to one twenty-eight for near fifty percent duty cycle; the LED will appear about half as bright as full on.
When precision matters
Smooth the PWM or use a DAC for low-ripple voltages in sensors or audio applications.
Key Takeaway

Treat analogWrite values as a fraction of two hundred fifty-five and compute average voltage when accuracy matters.

Quick checks
Use a multimeter to measure average voltage under PWM if you need verification; smoothing reduces ripple.
Common mistake
Assuming analogWrite value is linear with perceived brightness; human perception is nonlinear, so consider gamma or use lookup tables for smooth perceptual steps.

screens.title: Driving Motors with PWM
screens.subtitle: Safe wiring patterns and the role of transistors and drivers

narration.text: Motors draw more current than a microcontroller pin can safely provide, so you must use PWM through a transistor or motor driver to control speed. The Arduino provides the PWM timing, but a transistor, MOSFET, or dedicated driver provides the current-handling ability and protects the board. Always connect the motor and Arduino grounds together so the driver sees the same reference. For brushed DC motors use a transistor plus a flyback diode to absorb voltage spikes, or use an H-bridge driver if you need bidirectional control. A concrete wiring scenario: PWM from pin nine goes to the gate of a logic-level MOSFET; the motor connects between supply voltage and the MOSFET drain, and the MOSFET source goes to ground; include a diode across the motor and share ground with the Arduino. A common error is driving a motor directly from a digital pin which can damage the microcontroller. Also be aware that PWM frequency can affect audible motor noise; changing the PWM pin or using a driver with higher switching frequency can reduce hum. Takeaway: use the Arduino for timing and a properly rated switch or driver for power.

keyIdea.title: Motor control
keyIdea.text: Use PWM to command speed but switch motor current through a transistor or motor driver; always include flyback protection and shared ground.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Driving Motors with PWM
Safe motor wiring
The Arduino provides the PWM signal; use a transistor or driver to provide current and protect the board.
Scenario
Use a logic-level MOSFET as a low-side switch. PWM drives the gate, motor connects to supply, include a diode across the motor for flyback protection.
Driver options
Single MOSFET for one direction, H-bridge for reversible motors, or dedicated motor drivers for current sensing and braking.
Common mistake
Connecting a motor directly to an Arduino pin — it can exceed current limits and damage the microcontroller.
Key Takeaway

Always use a switch or driver for motors; the Arduino provides timing, not high current.

Quick checklist
  • Shared ground between Arduino and motor supply
  • Flyback diode across motor terminals
  • Properly rated MOSFET or driver

screens.title: tone() and noTone() for Buzzers
screens.subtitle: Generate square-wave tones and simple melodies using PWM pins

narration.text: Arduino's tone function produces a square wave at a given frequency on a pin, which is ideal for driving a piezo buzzer or small speaker for beeps and simple melodies. You specify the pin and frequency and optionally a duration. The noTone function stops any tone on a pin. A practical example: play a one thousand hertz beep for half a second to signal an event. Keep in mind that tone generates a square wave, which is a form of PWM — it's not high-fidelity audio. For small alarms and single-frequency beeps it is perfect, but for music or complex audio you will hear a harsh timbre because square waves contain many harmonics. Another point is that using tone on pins shared with PWM hardware may change behavior for analogWrite on those pins while the tone is active. A common misconception is that tone produces smooth audio like a DAC-based player; it does not. Takeaway: use tone for simple alarms and interactions; plan for a DAC or external audio hardware if you need quality sound. tone() and noTone() for Buzzers means tone() creates square-wave audio; use it for beeps and simple melodies, and stop it with notone().. screens.title: Potentiometer to LED: Real-time Control
screens.subtitle: Build the interactive circuit and code to control LED brightness and trigger a buzzer

narration.text: This hands-on activity ties the concepts together. Wire an LED through a resistor to a PWM pin, a potentiometer to an analog input, and a piezo buzzer to a spare digital pin. Begin by reading the potentiometer value and mapping it into the PWM range so you can call analogWrite with appropriate numbers. Update the LED in real time as the knob changes so the brightness follows smoothly. Add logic to check when the mapped brightness exceeds eighty percent; when that happens, play a short beep with tone for feedback and stop it with noTone when brightness falls below the threshold. Remember safety: shared grounds, correct resistor sizing, and using a transistor for loads that draw significant current. A common mistake is neglecting to debounce or filter noisy analog readings — apply short averaging if the LED flickers. This activity shows how inputs, mapping, PWM outputs, and simple audio interlock to create responsive controls. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: Why fades stutter, motors hum, and buzzers clash with PWM

narration.text: Troubleshooting PWM projects often comes down to a few repeated mistakes. First, forgetting to use a current-limiting resistor on LEDs or a transistor for motors causes heating and unreliable performance. Second, failing to tie grounds together leads to floating signals and unpredictable analogRead or PWM behavior. Third, using non-PWM pins for fades yields binary on/off behavior instead of smooth control. For motors, PWM frequency and driver type can make audible noise; if the motor hums, changing the PWM pin or using a higher-frequency driver can help. When a buzzer and PWM-driven LED share timers or pins, tones may interfere with analogWrite; test audio separately or reserve pins. Noisy analog inputs cause flickering fades — apply simple averaging or a small RC filter if needed. As a concrete debugging step, use a multimeter to read average voltage or observe an LED while you change values to see if behavior matches expectations. Takeaway: check wiring and hardware choices first, then code; many PWM problems are hardware-rooted. Troubleshooting checklist
Begin with wiring and hardware before changing software logic.

  • Floating ground: ensure all grounds are connected to the same reference.
  • Using wrong pin: confirm PWM pins on the board before using analogWrite for fading.

Debug step

Quick fixes
If LED flickers, add averaging or RC filtering. If motor hums, try a different PWM pin or a higher-frequency driver.
Key Takeaway

Start with hardware checks: resistors, grounds, drivers, and correct pins. Many problems disappear before you change code.

As a troubleshooting exercise, ask learners to describe what would happen if they used analogWrite on a non-PWM pin to dim an LED. screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarise the essential points you should remember. First, PWM is a rapid on/off signal whose duty cycle controls the average voltage a device senses; think time-based averaging rather than a change in instantaneous voltage. Second, the Arduino Uno only offers hardware PWM on pins three, five, six, nine, ten, and eleven, and those pins are marked on the board; use them for reliable analogWrite behavior. Third, analogWrite accepts values from zero to two hundred fifty-five; divide the value by two hundred fifty-five and multiply by your board voltage to estimate the average voltage. These three ideas — how PWM works, which pins to use, and how values map to average voltage — will guide safe wiring and correct code as you build LED fades, motor controllers, and simple buzzer outputs. Keep practicing the mapping and wiring checks until these habits become second nature.

keyIdea.text: PWM duty cycle, PWM pins, and analogWrite mapping are the practical core you will use most.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Key Concepts — Part 1
Key Concepts
Three quick reminders to carry forward.
PWM & Duty Cycle
On/off pulses averaged over time; duty cycle controls perceived output.
PWM Pins
Use pins 3,5,6,9,10,11 on the Uno; they are marked with a tilde.
analogWrite Mapping
Value ranges zero to two hundred fifty-five; value/255 × Vcc ≈ average voltage.
Final takeaway
PWM is a simple, effective way to control many actuators. Match hardware, pins, and logic to your project's needs.

narration.text: To finish, focus on three practical cautions. First, never drive high-current devices directly from a microcontroller pin; use transistors or drivers and include flyback diodes for inductive loads. Second, tone produces a square wave that is useful for alerts, but it is not a replacement for audio hardware when quality matters. Third, test and measure: a multimeter reading of average voltage and observing PWM behavior gives fast confirmation that wiring and code are doing what you expect. These small checks prevent damage and make behavior predictable as you scale your projects. As you practise, ask yourself: does this component respond to average energy, or does it need a constant voltage? That question steers the right design choice between PWM and a DAC. Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Key Concepts — Part 2
Final reminders
Three concise practical cautions to guide your work.
Use drivers for power
Switch current with transistors, MOSFETs, or drivers; include flyback diodes for motors.
tone is square wave
Great for beeps, not for high-fidelity audio; square waves contain many harmonics.
Measure and verify
Use a multimeter or simple oscilloscope to confirm average voltage and PWM behavior during debugging.
Parting thought
Ask whether your component responds to average power or requires a steady voltage — that decides PWM versus DAC.
